title-group.article-title: Leptomeningeal metastatic disease responding to carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab after progression to osimertinib in EGFR exon 21 L858R-Mutated non-small cell lung cancer: Two case reports

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Leptomeningeal metastatic disease (LMD) is associated with a poor prognosis in patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who experience disease progression after EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy. Amivantamab, an EGFR–mesenchymal-epithelial transition bispecific antibody, has demonstrated clinical efficacy in EGFR-mutated NSCLC; however, its effectiveness in treating symptomatic brain metastases and LMD remains unclear. We report on two cases of LMD that were managed with amivantamab. In Case 1, a 44-year-old woman developed symptomatic LMD during osimertinib therapy. Owing to prior prophylactic whole-brain irradiation during childhood, additional radiotherapy was not feasible. Carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab treatment resulted in remarkable LMD radiological improvement and gradual neurological symptom resolution. In Case 2, a 69-year-old man developed multiple asymptomatic brain metastases and LMD during osimertinib therapy. Second-line treatment with carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab resulted in a radiological response. To our knowledge, this is the first report to demonstrate the efficacy of carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab against LMD progression after osimertinib therapy, suggesting that this regimen may be a therapeutic option for patients with LMD, including those with symptomatic disease. Nevertheless, further studies are warranted to confirm efficacy in this population.

sec.p: Keywords: Amivantamab, Leptomeningeal metastatic disease, EGFR exon 21 L858R mutation, Non-small cell lung cancer

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Central nervous system (CNS) metastases from non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) may involve the brain parenchyma, leptomeninges, or both. Notably, CNS metastases are widespread in patients with metastatic NSCLC harboring epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations [1,2].

Osimertinib is among the standard first-line treatments for EGFR-mutated NSCLC and has demonstrated high CNS penetration, significant intracranial activity, and survival benefits in patients with brain metastases and leptomeningeal metastatic disease (LMD) [[3], [4], [5]]. Nevertheless, most patients eventually develop disease progression during osimertinib therapy.

Several phase III trials have evaluated second-line treatment strategies following osimertinib therapy, including carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab (MARIPOSA-2) [6]; carboplatin, paclitaxel, atezolizumab, and bevacizumab (ATTLAS) [7]; and carboplatin, pemetrexed, and ivonescimab (HARMONi-A) [8]. However, patients with LMD were excluded from these trials, and the efficacy of these regimens against LMD remains unknown.

Here, we report two EGFR exon 21 L858R–mutated NSCLC cases in which carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab demonstrated a radiographic response (plus a clinical improvement in Case 1) against LMD that developed during first-line osimertinib therapy.

sec.title: Case reports
sec.p: Case 1: A 44-year-old woman with no history of smoking was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, clinical stage T1bN3M0 (stage IIIB; eighth edition of the Union for International Cancer Control/American Joint Committee on Cancer Tumor, Node, Metastasis [TNM] classification). An EGFR exon 21 L858R mutation was identified. The patient received concurrent chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin, vinorelbine, and thoracic radiotherapy (60 Gy/30 fr), followed by maintenance durvalumab, and a partial response was achieved.

Twelve months after durvalumab initiation, computed tomography revealed multiple small pulmonary nodules consistent with recurrence. Osimertinib (80 mg/day) was initiated and resulted in a partial response. Fourteen months after osimertinib initiation, the patient developed neurological symptoms, including headache, nausea, anorexia, weight loss, and gait instability. Marked cerebellar leptomeningeal enhancement was noted on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; Fig. 1A); therefore, osimertinib was discontinued. Given the presence of characteristic MRI findings and clinical symptoms, cerebrospinal fluid analysis was not performed. At this time, the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG PS) of the patient was 1.

caption.p: LMD radiological course following carboplatin and pemetrexed plus amivantamab therapy initiation in case 1 (the hyperintense lesion observed in the right temporal lobe on MRI resonance imaging indicated a cavernous hemangioma). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences used for assessment was contrast-enhanced T1 and FLAIR, and response was assessed qualitatively.
(A) Baseline brain magnetic resonance imaging before carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab administration, exhibiting symptomatic leptomeningeal enhancement in the cerebellum.
(B) MRI at week 5 of treatment demonstrating no change in leptomeningeal enhancement in the cerebellum.
(C) MRI at week 11 of treatment demonstrates marked improvement in cerebellar leptomeningeal enhancement.
(D) MRI at week 17 of treatment demonstrates further improvement.

sec.p: Due to prior prophylactic whole-brain irradiation for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia, further radiotherapy was contraindicated in this patient. Second-line carboplatin (area under the curve [AUC], 5), pemetrexed (500 mg/m2), and amivantamab (following the MARIPOSA-2 trial protocol for patients weighing <80 kg) were initiated in August 2025. On day 1, a grade 3 (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0) infusion-related reaction (IRR) occurred, and amivantamab was interrupted after administration of 37.8 mg of the planned 350 mg dose, with no further dosing that day. On day 2, two grade 2 IRRs occurred, and amivantamab was interrupted after administration of 512.4 mg of the planned 1050 mg dose, with no further dosing that day. Amivantamab was administered on day 8 without IRR; however, dosing was discontinued on day 15 because of grade 3 febrile neutropenia. Cycle 2 was initiated in week 3 with dose reductions to carboplatin (AUC 3.75) and pemetrexed (375 mg/m2). After two cycles, the brain MRI conducted in week 5 exhibited no change in cerebellar leptomeningeal enhancement (Fig. 1B) and no LMD-related symptom improvement. Conversely, after four cycles, the patient's brain MRI at week 11 demonstrated a marked improvement in cerebellar leptomeningeal enhancement (Fig. 1C). Accordingly, the patient's grade 2 nausea resolved, oral intake increased, body weight recovered by 3 kg from a prior 6-kg loss, and gait instability improved. Treatment was ongoing when this report was written (December 28, 2025).

Case 2: A 69-year-old man with a 32 pack-year smoking history underwent right lower lobectomy for lung adenocarcinoma, pathologic stage T2aN0M0 (stage IB; eighth edition of the UICC/AJCC TNM classification). An EGFR exon 21 L858R mutation was identified. After 2 years of adjuvant oral tegafur–uracil, recurrence was detected with pleural dissemination, liver metastases, bone metastases, and multiple asymptomatic brain metastases.

Osimertinib (80 mg/day) was initiated, and a partial response was achieved. At 22 months, disease progression was identified, with new asymptomatic brain metastases and leptomeningeal enhancement observed on MRI (Fig. 2A). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was not performed, as the findings were unlikely to influence subsequent management. At this time, the ECOG PS of the patient was 1. Second-line carboplatin (AUC, 5), pemetrexed (500 mg/m2), and amivantamab (following the MARIPOSA-2 trial protocol for patients weighing <80 kg) was initiated in October 2025. On day 1, two grade 2 IRRs occurred, and amivantamab was interrupted after administration of 114.8 mg of the planned 350 mg dose, with no further dosing that day. Grade 3 elevations in the patient's aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase levels were observed, leading to discontinuation of amivantamab on days 8 and 15; these resolved after discontinuation of minocycline hydrochloride. From cycle 2 onward, treatment was administered without interruption. After three cycles, the patient's brain MRI at week 11 demonstrated reduced brain metastases and improved leptomeningeal enhancement (Fig. 2B). Treatment was ongoing when this report was written (December 28, 2025).

caption.p: LMD radiological course following initiation of carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab therapy in Case 2. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences used for assessment was contrast-enhanced T1 and FLAIR, and response was assessed qualitatively.

(A) Baseline brain magnetic resonance imaging before carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab administration showing asymptomatic leptomeningeal enhancement in the cerebrum (red arrowhead) and brain metastases (blue arrowheads).
(B) MRI at week 11 of treatment demonstrating radiographic shrinkage of both the leptomeningeal enhancement and brain metastases.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: LMD results from the dissemination of malignant cells into the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid, leading to neurological deficits, elevated intracranial pressure, and poor prognosis [[9], [10], [11]]. LMD incidence in NSCLC is approximately 2.8% overall, increasing to 9% in patients with EGFR-mutated tumors [12].

Before the advent of targeted therapies, the median overall survival of patients with LMD was limited to 2–5 months [[13], [14], [15]], with symptomatic individuals exhibiting inferior outcomes. Although osimertinib improves CNS control, the treatment options following progression to osimertinib, particularly for LMD, remain limited.

Amivantamab, an EGFR–mesenchymal-epithelial transition bispecific antibody, demonstrated significantly better progression-free survival and intracranial benefits when combined with chemotherapy in the MARIPOSA-2 trial. Patients with symptomatic brain metastases or LMD were excluded. Similarly, the ATTLAS and HARMONi-A studies excluded symptomatic brain metastases and LMD, leaving treatment for LMD after progression to osimertinib as an unmet need.

Kim et al. [16] reported a case of NSCLC harboring EGFR G719A and A289V mutations, in which amivantamab monotherapy demonstrated marked efficacy against brain metastases and LMD after the progression of LMD during osimertinib treatment. The response was sustained for >19 months, with complete resolution of both brain metastases and LMD by month 6, underscoring the potential activity of amivantamab against LMD progression during osimertinib therapy. Nonetheless, to date, no reports have described carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab efficacy for treating the progression of LMD during osimertinib treatment in patients with common EGFR mutations. Therefore, the significant LMD responses to carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab observed in these cases are clinically meaningful.

Chen et al. [17] reported a phase II study evaluating amivantamab plus lazertinib in patients with brain or leptomeningeal metastases previously treated for EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Overall, 41 patients were enrolled; 90% had received osimertinib as prior therapy, and 21 patients had LMD. In this cohort, 41%, 37%, 12%, and 10% harbored an EGFR exon 19 deletion, a L858R mutation, an exon 20 insertion, and uncommon EGFR mutations, respectively. The LMD objective response rate, assessed using a combination of the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors and the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology criteria, was 33% (95% confidence interval [CI], 15–57%). In the LMD cohort, median progression-free survival was 7.8 months (95% CI, 4.2–12.2), and median overall survival was 14.4 months (95% CI, 8.9–not reached). Therefore, amivantamab-based regimens may provide radiographically meaningful activity against LMD after progression to osimertinib. To date, the mechanism by which amivantamab exerts therapeutic efficacy in LMD remains unclear; therefore, further research is warranted.

In conclusion, we reported two cases of EGFR exon 21 L858R–mutated NSCLC with LMD that developed after progression to osimertinib and responded markedly to carboplatin, pemetrexed, and amivantamab treatment. This regimen may be a viable treatment option for patients with LMD, a population largely excluded from clinical trials. Further studies are warranted to elucidate the efficacy of amivantamab-containing regimens for LMD after progression to osimertinib.
